question: A 65-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of sudden, worsening pain in his right calf and foot that started 30 minutes ago. He also has a tingling sensation and weakness in his right leg. He has had no similar episodes, recent trauma, or claudication. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus and was diagnosed with hypertension 20 years ago. His sister has systemic sclerosis. He works as an office administrator and sits at his desk most of the day. He has smoked one and a half packs of cigarettes daily for 30 years. Current medications include metformin and lisinopril. His pulse is 110/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. His right leg is pale and cool to touch. Muscle strength in his right leg is mildly reduced. Pedal pulses are absent on the right. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's symptoms?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Atherosclerotic narrowing of the artery -> Reduced blood flow to the right leg -> Ischemia -> Pain, tingling, and weakness in the right calf and foot -> Absent pedal pulses on the right -> 80% confidence. CHAIN: Arterial embolism -> Sudden blockage of blood flow to the right leg -> Ischemia -> Pain, tingling, and weakness in the right calf and foot -> Absent pedal pulses on the right -> 70% confidence. CHAIN: Atheroembolism -> Embolus from atherosclerotic plaque -> Blockage of blood flow to the right leg -> Ischemia -> Pain, tingling, and weakness in the right calf and foot -> Absent pedal pulses on the right -> 80%
enhanced_information: The most likely underlying cause of this patient's symptoms is arterial embolism. The sudden blockage of blood flow to the right leg resulting in ischemia, pain, tingling, weakness in the right calf and foot, and absent pedal pulses on the right align with this diagnosis. Atherosclerotic narrowing of the artery and atheroembolism are less likely based on the clinical presentation and absence of relevant risk factors.
analysis: The patient's presentation of sudden onset pain, tingling, weakness, absent pedal pulses, and coolness in the right leg is highly suggestive of acute limb ischemia. The most likely underlying cause in this scenario is arterial embolism, which can acutely block blood flow to the leg. Atherosclerotic narrowing of the artery and atheroembolism are less likely given the acute nature of the symptoms and absence of relevant risk factors like a history of claudication. Popliteal artery aneurysm could present similarly but is less common in this context.
